1.pericope_label: Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God

schools.summary: Gill takes the title to include the three offices of prophet, priest and king; Calvin holds that the title designates the office appointed by the Father, that Christ cannot be received unless salvation is sought from him, and that all who really believe have first been born of God.
Henry makes the verse a third reason for brotherly love, the eminent relation of those loved, and infers that sonship is no longer confined to Abraham’s seed after the flesh.

Robertson identifies the contemporary denial as one that separates Jesus from the Christ, insists on full surrender rather than intellectual conviction, quotes the judgment that the divine begetting precedes the believing, and parses the closing participles as the Father and the fellow-believer.

Clarke joins the two halves of the verse, the believer who confides in Christ for remission being begotten of God and loving all God’s children in return; Wesley takes the scope of the paragraph from its conclusion and observes that faith is the first and last point with this apostle.
Cyril of Jerusalem locates the point of denial precisely, that the Jews allow he is Jesus but not that he is Christ, and expounds a priesthood held by no bodily succession and confirmed by an oath.

Augustine of Hippo continues the previous day’s exposition, defines unbelief as failure to live as Christ commanded since faith without works does not save, and figures wrong works as running hard but off the road, so that the more a man runs the further he goes astray.

debates: Which comes first, believing or being begotten: Robertson and Calvin both make the divine begetting antecedent to the faith, while Clarke states the sequence the other way, the begetting following on belief and confidence in Christ for pardon.
outliers: Augustine of Hippo treats the verse as a test of life rather than of profession, defining the unbeliever as the man who does not live as Christ commanded.
themes: believing that Jesus is the Christ

2.pericope_label: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the test needs stating in this direction, since carnal friendships regard only private advantage or some vanishing object, so that the apostle having given the effect now gives the cause and mutual love must be cultivated so that God is honoured; Gill flags a version that turns the clause into a tautology, proving the same by the same.

Barnes reads the verse as reversing the usual test, since love to God may be known directly by consciousness and by pleasure in his perfections, and love to the brethren inferred from it, and answers the objection that men may love Christians from motives that are not religious at all; Robertson quotes the judgment that the two loves each include the other so that each is a test of the other, and notes the indefinite temporal construction.

Clarke compresses the whole into a chain, love of God’s followers proving love to God, love to God causing love to his children, and obedience proving love to him; Wesley calls the verse a plain proof.

outliers: Barnes raises against himself the objection that love to Christians ought to be easier to ascertain than love to God, and answers it from the mixed motives on which men love one another.
themes: love of God and of the brethren

3.pericope_label: This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous

schools.summary: Calvin joins reverence to love as inseparable, since God is the fountain of righteousness and cannot be divided from himself, cautions that obedience under constraint of fear is not true obedience, and alone states in full the objection that the yoke of the law is insupportable, answering that the difficulty lies in our corrupt flesh and not in the nature of the law; Gill takes the keeping as evidence that love is not in word and tongue only but in deed and truth.

Barnes glosses the word as heavy and holds that the laws are neither unreasonable nor beyond our ability, that complaints come only from the unwilling, and that no true Christian ever called them stern, the service of God being freedom and the service of the world bondage; Robertson calls obedience the supreme test, reads the construction as explanatory against mere declamatory boasting, and says love for God lightens his commands.

Clarke answers through a proverb, that love feels no loads since no man is burdened by the duties his own love imposes, adds that love to God brings strength from God so that the commandments become delightful, and quotes a rabbinic saying that a man can bring God no worship but love; Wesley adds the qualification that they are not grievous to any that are born of God.

debates: Whether the commandments really are light: Barnes and Clarke take the claim at face value and treat complaints as evidence of an unwilling heart, while Calvin sets the words against the passages calling the yoke insupportable and locates the whole difficulty in the flesh rather than the law.
outliers: Calvin alone insists that obedience rendered only under constraint of fear does not count as keeping the commandments at all.
themes: the difficulty located in the flesh

4.pericope_label: Whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory, even our faith

schools.summary: Calvin reports and then declines the view that the neuter was chosen to include all sorts of persons, calling it a peculiarity of style not to be preserved in translation, fastens on the past tense as speaking of an enemy already put to flight so that fear is removed though the warfare lasts all life, and notes that victory stands for what brings victory; Gill allows the phrase to cover either the persons born of God or the principle of grace in them.

Robertson explains the neuter as sharpening the universality of the principle, defines the world as the sum of the forces antagonistic to the spiritual life, reads the present tense as continuous victory in a continuous struggle and the aorist as singling out an individual experience, and notes that the noun for victory occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Barnes makes the phrase mean that every true regeneration carries this victory, so that where the spirit of the world reigns supreme there is no true religion.

Clarke reports the opinion that the world here means Judaism, with two reasons for it, before offering the ordinary reading as an alternative; Wesley reads the neuter as implying the most unlimited universality.

debates: What the world means here: Clarke preserves the reading that confines it to the Jewish religion, on the ground that it was this world which denied the Messiah had come, while Robertson and Barnes take it for the whole sum of forces hostile to the spiritual life.
outliers: Calvin and Robertson both fasten on the tense, Calvin taking the past as assurance that the enemy is already routed and Robertson taking it as marking the moment an individual met temptation and won.

5.pericope_label: Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God?

schools.summary: Calvin supplies the reason the victory belongs to faith, that we conquer by deriving strength from Christ, so that only the man who distrusts himself and rests on Christ’s power overcomes, faith meaning a real apprehension of him by which we apply his power to ourselves; Gill reads the question as a strong affirmation that no other person is the conqueror of the world.

Robertson takes the question as an appeal to experience and fact rather than rhetoric, and finds a sharp antithesis between the human name and the divine title united in one personality; Barnes presses the appeal by granting every partial reform short of faith, the abandoned circle, the sobered passions, the withdrawal from politics, the emperor laying down office, and denying that any of them overcomes the world.
Clarke defines the belief in question as belief in a Messiah supernaturally generated, truly man yet not by man; Wesley answers the question in four words, every believer and none else.

outliers: Barnes concedes the reality of every partial victory over particular vices in order to deny that any of them amounts to overcoming the world.
themes: the question as appeal to fact

6.pericope_label: This is he that came by water and blood, even Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Gill rules out the ceremonial washings, Christ’s own purity and the cleansing of his people before settling on water baptism, since it was at Jordan that he was made manifest; Calvin dissents, judging a reference to baptism improbable and taking the water from the pierced side, and reads the pair typologically as the washing and the expiation of the law, so that Christ brings the substance of what the rites shadowed.

Henry matches the two to two defilements, the inward pollution of sin in our nature requiring a spiritual water that can reach the soul, and treats both as at once the notes of a true Saviour and the means by which he saves.

Robertson explains why these two incidents are singled out, the formal setting apart at the baptism and the culmination at the Cross, argues from the repeated preposition and article for two separate events with emphasis on the blood, and finds in the water and blood from the pierced side a refutation both of the denial of a human body and of the separation of Jesus from the Christ; Barnes guards against reading the phrase as accompaniment and illustrates the idiom from ambassadors, warriors, princes and prophets.

Clarke takes the water for the baptism where the Spirit descended and the voice was heard, and the blood for the sacrificial death, and adds a comparison with Moses who came by water and Aaron who came by blood; Wesley holds the two together as an undertaking at the baptism accomplished at the cross, and closes on the Spirit testifying by Moses, the prophets, the Baptist and the apostles.

debates: What the water means: Gill, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley all take it for the baptism at Jordan, while Calvin says outright that a reference to baptism is not probable and takes it from the water that flowed from the pierced side.
outliers: Robertson reads the emphasis on the blood as polemical, aimed at teachers who made light of it, and treats the flow from the side as decisive against two distinct early errors at once.
themes: the shadows of the law fulfilled

7.pericope_label: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost

schools.summary: Gill answers the objections one by one, arguing that the Syriac is only a version and a defective one which formerly lacked several whole books until they were supplied from later copies, as this verse has since been; Calvin reports the omission and one father’s suspicion that it was deliberate, declines to assert anything since the Greek copies disagree, and is inclined to receive the clause because the passage flows better with it and because he finds it in the copies he judges best.

Barnes explains why this verse above all others has been disputed, the doctrinal stake making both sides unwilling to yield, prints the passage with the words bracketed, and judges them spurious on the ground that no Greek copy before the sixteenth century contains them; Robertson traces the addition to a Latin scribe copying an early exegesis into his margin and to the editor of the first printed Greek Testament accepting a manuscript produced as if to order, and insists that neither the fact nor the doctrine of the Trinity depends on it.

Clarke gives the full count of manuscripts and versions that lack the words, a hundred and twelve copies and every ancient version but the Latin, and prints the passage twice so the reader can see what is added, concluding that the verse is likely not genuine, though he states what the three witnesses are said to do and that they are one in essence; Wesley defends the verse on the critical work of a contemporary scholar and rates it as high as anything in the epistle.

debates: Whether the verse belongs to the text: Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all judge it an addition and give manuscript grounds, Gill and Wesley defend it and answer the objections, and Calvin declines to decide while leaning to receive it on grounds of sense and of the copies available to him.
outliers: Robertson separates the textual question from the doctrinal one entirely, holding that the Trinity is untouched by whether the clause stands or falls.

8.pericope_label: And there are three that bear witness in earth, the spirit, the water, and the blood

schools.summary: Calvin explains why a third witness is added and gives the Spirit the first place though he is named last, since without him the water and blood would have flowed without benefit, and it is he who seals their testimony on the heart and makes the fruit of Christ’s death reach us; he supports it from Paul’s joining the resurrection to the sanctification of the Spirit, without whom every sign of divine glory in Christ would escape our sight; Gill notes that the three witness to the same truth, the sonship of Christ.

Barnes holds that the words in earth must fall with the interpolation they were framed to answer, so that the genuine sentence names only the Spirit, the water and the blood, and lists the occasions on which the Spirit bore his witness, from the baptism of Jesus to the conversion of individuals now; Robertson reads the clause as a resumption with the Spirit placed first and takes the closing phrase to mean that the three are for one purpose, faith in Jesus as the incarnate Son of God.

Clarke adopts and attributes to Wesley the account of the three as the Spirit in the word confirmed by miracles, the water in baptism and the blood in the Lord’s Supper, and then presses each as a witness still testifying now, in the written word, in a rite still maintained and in a sacrament that shows forth the atoning death until he comes; the comment printed under Wesley’s name here belongs to the heavenly witnesses of the other verse.

outliers: Calvin inverts the order of the verse, making the witness named last the one on which the other two depend for any effect at all.

9.pericope_label: If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater

schools.summary: Calvin states the argument as one from the less to the greater and concludes that only our own corruption prevents us receiving Christ, and widens the divine testimony to include what we derive from the water and the blood, since their cleansing power was heavenly, so that the blood of Christ must be estimated by God’s design rather than in the common manner of men; Gill lists the human witnesses actually credited about Christ, the wise men, the shepherds and the Baptist.
Henry turns the comparison into a charge, that nothing is more absurd than doubting the truth of Christianity while proceeding without hesitation on human testimony in the common affairs of life.

Barnes develops at length how universally men act on the testimony of others and how the world would halt if that credence ceased, then lists the ways men may deceive or be deceived of which God is incapable; Robertson supplies the legal conditions for a valid witness and passes on the observation that the Son comes, the Spirit witnesses and the Father has witnessed.

Clarke compresses the contrast into a clause, that God can neither be deceived nor deceive while man may do both; Wesley notes that we accept human testimony continually and identifies the divine testimony as that borne of the Son as Saviour of the world.

outliers: Calvin refuses to confine the witness of God to the inward impression of the Spirit, counting the water and the blood as divine testimony too on the ground that their power was not earthly.
themes: from the less to the greater

10.pericope_label: He that believeth on the Son of God hath the witness in himself

schools.summary: Calvin says the apostle does not speak of God speaking outwardly but of every godly man feeling within that God is the author of his faith, which is what distinguishes faith from a fading opinion resting on something else, and makes the unbeliever guilty of extreme blasphemy in robbing God of the honour of his truth; Gill describes the faith as believing in Christ for righteousness and eternal life.

Henry catalogues what the believer can allege from his own experience, the sight of his sin and need, the fitness of the Saviour, the wisdom and love of God in sending him, and the felt power of his word, and adds that the assurance puts the matter beyond doubt except in hours of darkness or conflict.

Barnes denies that the inward witness is an immediate revelation independent of the external evidence, making it the fruit of all evidence working on the heart, and lists what that conviction rests on, from peace in believing to the disarming of death; Robertson finds a deliberate distinction between believing God and believing into the Son, notes the perfect tenses as marking a permanent state, and that the reason for the charge is actual rather than supposed.

Clarke states the inward witness without qualification, the Spirit bearing witness with a man’s spirit that he is a child of God, so that to know and feel sin forgiven on the Holy Spirit’s own testimony is the privilege of every true believer; Wesley states the mechanism of unbelief plainly, that such a man supposes to be false what God has expressly testified.

debates: What the inward witness is: Barnes insists it is the cumulative effect of evidence outward and inward and expressly not an immediate revelation, while Clarke and Calvin both describe a testimony given within by the Spirit himself and distinguished from anything resting on external grounds.
outliers: Calvin makes unbelief not merely an error but the gravest possible injury to God, since it robs him of the honour he values above all, his own truth.
themes: believing God and believing on the Son
unbelief as calling God a liar

11.pericope_label: This is the record, that God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son

schools.summary: Gill takes the record as covering both the person of Christ and the security of salvation in him; Calvin reads the verse as an invitation rather than a statement, holds that the gospel is to be loved and not merely obeyed reverently because it brings eternal life, and infers that the free gift of salvation is what is chiefly to be sought there, the calls to repentance and fear not being separable from the grace of Christ.

Barnes calls the verse the sum of the testimony God has given respecting his Son, life provided through the Saviour and treasured up in him; Robertson notes the aorist marking the historic fact of the Incarnation where a perfect is used earlier for the abiding presence of God’s love, and observes that eternal life stands here without the article and so emphasises quality.

Clarke calls it the great truth to which the three witnesses testify and defines the gift as both a right to endless glory and a meetness for it, concluding that no other scheme of salvation can be effectual; Wesley finds both a title to eternal life and the real beginning of it in the same phrase, communicated from the fulness of the Son to his body first in grace and then in glory.

outliers: Calvin turns the statement into a duty of affection, arguing that reverent obedience to the gospel is not enough where what it brings is eternal life.

12.pericope_label: He that hath the Son hath life; and he that hath not the Son of God hath not life

schools.summary: Gill describes having the Son as a spiritual and experimental knowledge of him with Christ dwelling in the heart; Calvin treats the verse as closing every other door, since it might have sufficed that God placed life in Christ alone, and alone raises the case of great men of heroic virtue wholly unacquainted with Christ, answering that what is highly esteemed among men is abomination with God, since the filthiness of the heart is hidden from us while God sees beneath the appearance.

Barnes traces the sentence to a saying of the Saviour himself and reads it as the sense of all the testimony God ever bore on salvation, the believer already possessing the elements of eternal life and the unbeliever failing to attain it; Robertson identifies the life as the one God gave in the previous verse and as the position Jesus takes in the Gospel.

Clarke presses the exclusion into a rule and warns against evading it, since an indwelling Christ gives both the title and the meetness and it is vain to expect glory without him; Wesley explains the change from the Son to the Son of God between the clauses as addressed first to believers who know him and then to unbelievers who may learn what they fall short of.

outliers: Calvin alone confronts the case of virtuous men outside Christ, and answers by denying that human estimates of eminence carry any weight with God.

13.pericope_label: These things have I written that ye may know that ye have eternal life

schools.summary: Calvin builds a doctrine of progress on the verse, that faith needs daily increase and that what we believe is not really believed until it is more fully confirmed, and specifies the means as exposition of the office and power of Christ rather than exhortation in general; Gill takes the reference widely, to the epistle as a whole and to the witnesses just rehearsed.

Henry states the conclusion the chapter has been building toward, that on all this evidence it is right to believe on the name of the Son of God, and that we should thankfully receive the record of Scripture knowing our labour is not in vain.

Robertson refers the aorist to the twelve verses just finished, notes that the verb for knowing means settled intuitive knowledge, and cautions against a flippant superficiality in that assurance; Barnes glosses believing on the name as believing on the person, reads the second purpose as perseverance rather than commencement, and makes it a chief duty of ministers to secure the perseverance of real Christians; Ellicott measures the purpose against the Gospel, where the aim was that they might believe and have life, and finds this more positive, that they may know they have it.

Clarke says he writes to show their privileges and lead them into the holy of holies, defines believing as an actual enjoyment of salvation rather than a blind reliance for it, and lays out a chain in which faith lives by love and love continues by obedience, each link implying the next; Wesley notes the change of tense between the opening of the letter and its close and reads the purpose as a fuller and stronger assurance.

outliers: Calvin makes the letter an argument for continuing education in faith, holding that doctrine is for confirming the taught as much as for instructing the ignorant.

14.pericope_label: This is the confidence that we have in him, that if we ask any thing according to his will he heareth us

schools.summary: Calvin makes boldness in prayer the chief evidence and the chief trial of faith, holds that God is not rightly called upon unless we are fully persuaded our prayers will not be in vain, and charges a whole system of religion in his own day with burying the doctrine of faith by taking all certainty away; Gill glosses the confidence as boldness and liberty of speech, exercised under the sprinkling of Christ’s blood.
Henry sets the boundary from the other side, that it is not fit we should ask what is contrary either to God’s majesty and glory or to our own good, since we are his and dependent on him.

Barnes confines the confidence to the answering of prayer and calls the limiting clause the proper and necessary condition of all prayer, since no man could hope for good who preferred his own wishes to God’s will; Robertson takes the preposition for fellowship face to face, calls the qualifying phrase the secret of all prayer, true even in the case of Jesus, and observes that God hears even when he does not grant what is asked.

Clarke renders the word as liberty of access and speech, calls prayer the language of the children of God and of dependence on him, and identifies the will in question with what God has revealed and promised, so that faith and prayer are not to advance claims boldly on their own; Wesley reads hearing as favourable regard.

outliers: Calvin turns the verse into a polemic, treating the certainty the apostle requires as the very thing a rival system condemns, and taking that for proof the doctrine of faith is buried there.
themes: prayer as the trial of faith

15.pericope_label: If we know that he hear us, we know that we have the petitions that we desired of him

schools.summary: Gill notes only that God hears and answers all such as ask according to his will.

Henry states the comfort plainly, that to know one’s petitions are heard or accepted is as good as knowing they are answered, and lists what the holy petitioner needs, to be pitied, pardoned, counselled, sanctified, assisted and saved.

Barnes argues that knowing we have the petitions cannot mean already possessing what is asked, since much that is prayed for is future, a journey, a harvest, a recovery, a son’s safe return, and takes it to mean that we shall have them, resting the argument on the faithfulness of God, so that where the specific thing is withheld the prayer is still not disregarded and what is most for our good is given.

Clarke reaches the same conclusion by a shorter route, that the petitions may be counted as sure as if we already had them and will be had as soon as we need them, since God does not give today’s needed mercy tomorrow but gives it when it is needful.

outliers: Barnes distinguishes between the petition being granted and the particular thing being given, so that an unanswered request and a disregarded prayer are not the same.

16.pericope_label: If any man see his brother sin a sin which is not unto death, he shall ask, and he shall give him life

schools.summary: Calvin declines to identify the sin and attends to the temper the passage might produce, treating the falls of brethren as stimulants to prayer, calling it an iron hardness to feel no pity for souls going to ruin, and warning against both the cruelty of condemning brethren and an extreme rigour in despairing of them; Gill defines the brother rather than the sin, as one judged born again and under the watch of the saints.
Henry holds that we cannot pray for the forgiveness of the impenitent while they remain such, but may pray for their repentance and faith and on that ground for every other saving mercy.

Barnes lists six opinions on what the sin unto death is without endorsing any, from the sin against the Holy Ghost to offences the magistrate could not pardon, and draws from the bare list the impropriety of much confidence in one’s own judgment; Robertson accepts the distinction as real, supports it from rabbinic usage and the Greek Old Testament, connects it with the unpardonable sin and with those who set themselves up as antichrists, and denies that prayer is forbidden here.

Clarke sets out three chief opinions, the Jewish legal distinction between capital offences and sins of ignorance and the civil distinction between crimes admitting no pardon and those a magistrate may commute, and draws the moral that men should use their influence for the wretched; Wesley defines the sin as total apostasy from both the power and form of godliness, allows a second sense, and reads the clause as a prohibition of prayer.

debates: Whether prayer is forbidden: Wesley reads the clause as a prohibition and says outright that a man is not to pray for such a case, while Robertson denies that John forbids it at all and holds he merely refrains from commanding it, leaving the matter to God; Henry proposes a middle course, praying not for pardon but for repentance.

What the sin unto death is: Barnes catalogues six views and endorses none, Clarke three, Robertson favours a link with the unpardonable sin and with apostates turned antichrist, and Wesley defines it as total apostasy from the power and form of godliness.
outliers: Calvin sets the danger on the other side from most, warning less against praying wrongly than against a rigour that despairs of a brother’s salvation.

17.pericope_label: All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death

schools.summary: Calvin canvasses three ways of construing the sentence, adversatively, consecutively, or by taking the unrighteousness as complete unrighteousness and so the summit of sin, and declines to choose between the first two since the result is nearly the same; Gill illustrates from cases, that David’s sins were unrighteousness against God and man and yet were put away, and that Peter sinned very foully and was given repentance unto life.

Barnes reads the verse as thrown in to guard the last, preventing the inference that because one enormous sin cannot be forgiven, sin as such is unpardonable, since everything unrighteous is sin without all sin being of that character; Robertson turns it outward, that the world takes sin too lightly, even jokingly, as a mere animal inheritance, whereas sin is a terrible reality, though there is no cause for despair since sin not unto death can be overcome in Christ.

Wesley states both halves in one line, that all deviation from perfect holiness is sin but not all sin is unpardonable; Clarke defines the term simply as every act contrary to justice, a transgression of the law that condemns all injustice.

outliers: Robertson uses the verse against his own contemporaries rather than the apostle’s, treating a light view of sin as the modern error the sentence corrects.

18.pericope_label: Whosoever is born of God sinneth not, but keepeth himself, and that wicked one toucheth him not

schools.summary: Calvin names the fanatics who suppose God’s children wholly free from all sin and argues that such a reading would contradict the command to pray for one another, taking the sense to be that they do not wholly fall away, and reads the last clause of a deadly wound warded off by the shield of faith so that spiritual life is never extinguished; Gill describes the man in question as regenerated, quickened and having Christ formed in him.

Henry reads the security as reaching precisely the sin just discussed, since the new nature and the indwelling Spirit prevent the admission of unpardonable sin, and takes the clause about keeping as an indication of power conferred in regeneration rather than a bare statement of duty.

Barnes limits the denial to habitual and final sin and infers that a true Christian cannot commit the unpardonable sin and so cannot fall from grace, while insisting we never stop praying for one who has fallen; Robertson reads the present tense as not continuing in sin, and dissents from the usual construction by taking the participle for Christ, so that it is he who keeps the one begotten of God, and reads the closing verb as a grasp rather than a touch.

Clarke states without qualification that adult Christians are cleansed from all unrighteousness and consequently from all sin, glosses the keeping as building oneself up on faith and praying in the Holy Ghost, and explains that the devil finds nothing of his own nature to work on; Wesley qualifies by duration rather than degree, so long as that loving faith abides, and limits the touching to touching so as to hurt.

debates: Who keeps whom: Gill, Clarke, Calvin, Wesley and Henry all read the believer as keeping himself, while Robertson argues from the manuscripts and from the change of participle that Christ is the one who keeps him.

How far freedom from sin extends: Clarke says adult Christians are cleansed from all sin, while Calvin names that view as the fanatics’ and holds it would make the apostle contradict his own command to pray for the brethren.
outliers: Barnes turns the verse into an argument for perseverance, reasoning that a man who cannot commit the unpardonable sin cannot finally fall away.

19.pericope_label: We know that we are of God, and the whole world lieth in wickedness

schools.summary: Gill specifies how the first certainty is known, by the Spirit witnessing with the spirits of the saints and by the fruits of regenerating grace such as love to the brethren, and sets the two halves of the verse against each other.

Barnes holds that true Christians may have evidence clear enough to leave no doubt of their sonship, argues that the disputed word is masculine and means the wicked one rather than wickedness, giving two reasons for it, and defines the world as the people of the earth rather than the material creation; Robertson agrees on the masculine and calls the clause a terrible picture of the Graeco-Roman world of the first century, confirmed by Paul and by the pagan writers of the period.

Clarke calls the first clause the fullest proof of the truth of Christianity and of our reconciliation to God, adopts the masculine rendering and presses the figure of a world asleep in the arms of the wicked one and drawing its heat from him, and expands a remark of Wesley’s into a catalogue of the actions, conversation, contracts, quarrels and friendships of worldly men.

debates: Whether the closing word is neuter or masculine: the common rendering makes the world lie in wickedness, while Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all read the wicked one, Barnes arguing it from the parallel phrase in the next verse.
outliers: Clarke turns the clause into a description of ordinary social life, reading the falsity of contracts, quarrels and friendships as evidence of whose arms the world is lying in.
themes: in wickedness or in the wicked one

20.pericope_label: We know that the Son of God is come: this is the true God, and eternal life

schools.summary: Calvin makes the verse structural, reminding those under assault where their knowledge is to be found, since faith not founded on God will never stand firm, and presses the adjective as meaning not one who tells the truth but one who really is God, set against all idols; Gill lists what made the coming knowable, the apostles seeing and handling him and the prophetic marks of the time being past.

Barnes denies that the understanding given is a new faculty and traces all right knowledge of God to the Prophet he sent, then treats at length the question whether the closing demonstrative refers to Christ or to the Father, deciding for Christ on the evidence of this writer’s own language elsewhere and on the ground that any other reading would have misled readers into the very sin forbidden in the next verse, so that the clause is a direct assertion of Christ’s divinity; he also notes a variant inserting the word God which he judges insufficiently attested; Robertson takes the clause about the Son as explaining how we are in the True One rather than standing in apposition, and grants that the demonstrative is grammatically open.

Clarke calls the understanding a more eminent degree of light than was ever enjoyed before and holds that through this revelation we know the Trinity in the undivided unity of the Godhead; Wesley states without argument that this Jesus is the only living and true God together with the Father and the Spirit, and observes that the beginning and end of the epistle agree.

debates: To whom the closing words refer: Barnes argues at length that the demonstrative points to Christ and treats the sentence as a direct assertion of his divinity, while Robertson allows that it may grammatically refer either to Christ or to the True One.
outliers: Barnes argues from the danger of misunderstanding, holding that the words would have led men to worship a creature as God unless Christ is himself divine.

21.pericope_label: Little children, keep yourselves from idols

schools.summary: Gill extends the word by stages from heathen idols and meats sacrificed in their temples to images brought in by nominal Christians, to false doctrines, to the lusts of the heart, and finally to every creature loved too much, since covetousness is called idolatry, and reads the passage as an antidote against image-worship afterwards introduced; Calvin holds that the apostle commands us to beware of all images and not merely of idolatry, since superstition is so innate that the least occasion infects us, calls images sparks or rather torches able to set the world alight, extends the word to altars and every instrument of superstition, and rejects as ridiculous any attempt to confine the verse to pagan statues.

Barnes notes the affectionate address as characteristic and says the parting counsel embraces the whole letter, since all its aims would be met if nothing estranged their hearts from God, and defines an idol as a representation of the Deity made an object of worship, so that the word covers images of the true God as well as heathen deities; Robertson observes that the reflexive is neuter to match the address and that the active voice accents the effort required, idolatry being everywhere and the peril great.

Clarke turns the command into instruction, no idols in the house, the church or the heart, and lists what may serve as one from relics and crosses to wealth, fame, furniture, books, titles and human friendships, his rule being that a man’s idol is whatever he seeks his happiness from; he adds the original occasion, the temptation to eat of the temple feasts, and cites an old English version that rendered the word by a term for dolls; Wesley runs the same ladder from false gods to images to every inward idol, anything loved or feared more than God.

outliers: Calvin alone makes the verse a rule about the means of worship rather than its object, holding that religion is corrupted whenever a bodily form is ascribed to God at all.
